chapters.title: Chapter 5: Market Microstructure and Execution Mechanics

lessons.title: Order Types Market Makers Use: Limit, Iceberg, and Immediate-or-Cancel on NSE

body.text: Reservation prices, skewing, and inventory limits are all decisions made in theory. NSE only understands a handful of concrete order types, and turning a quoting strategy into an actual working system means knowing exactly which one to reach for at each moment.

children.text: Almost everything this course has described so far, a market maker's bid, its ask, its skewed reservation price, is expressed on NSE through a plain limit order: a specified price, a specified quantity, and a validity that is either Day, meaning it rests until filled, cancelled, or the session ends, or Immediate-or-Cancel, covered next. A market maker's continuous two-sided quote is, mechanically, nothing more than a pair of limit orders sitting in the book, one on the bid side and one on the ask side, that get cancelled and replaced constantly as fair value and inventory change.
Immediate-or-Cancel: Trading Now Without Leaving a Trace

markDefs.definition: An order validity type that fills as much quantity as is immediately available at the specified price or better, the instant it reaches the exchange, and automatically cancels whatever portion could not be filled right away rather than letting it rest in the book.

children.text: order takes whatever is available and cancels the rest instantly, with no resting exposure. Recall the aggressive unwind from Chapter 3's third lesson: a market maker choosing to pay the spread to flatten a position quickly does not want to accidentally leave a partially filled order sitting in the book afterward, priced at a level that may no longer reflect where it wants to be. Sending that unwind as an IOC order guarantees exactly that outcome: it either fills against whatever is currently resting on the other side, up to the specified price, or the unfilled part disappears immediately rather than lingering as an unintended resting quote.

body.text: If the same 300-unit order had instead requested 500 units, only 300 would fill across the first two levels, and the remaining 200 would be cancelled immediately rather than resting at ₹85.20 waiting for more sellers, since IOC orders never rest under any circumstances.

children.text: Iceberg Orders: Hiding the Real Size Being Worked

markDefs.definition: A large order that only shows a specified portion of its total quantity in the visible order book at any time; as that visible portion trades, the exchange automatically refreshes it from the hidden remainder, until the full order is worked or cancelled.

children.text: NSE supports this through its Disclosed Quantity (DQ) facility, commonly called an

: a trader working a large total quantity specifies a much smaller disclosed portion, and the exchange shows only that smaller portion in the depth window, refreshing it from the undisclosed remainder each time it trades. This directly addresses the signalling problem raised in Chapter 3's third lesson: an aggressive unwind of a large position, sent as one visibly large order, tells every other participant watching the tape exactly how much urgency and size is behind it. The same total size worked through an iceberg order lets other market makers and desks see only a fraction of it at a time, reducing how much of the market maker's true position and urgency leaks into the tape while it is being worked.

children.text: Day Validity and the Reality of Continuous Requoting

It is worth being precise here: NSE's standard order validities for ordinary trading are Day and Immediate-or-Cancel, not a multi-day standing order that persists unattended across sessions. A market maker's quote that appears continuously present across an entire session, or across many sessions, is not one single resting order; it is the market maker's own system placing a fresh Day order, then cancelling and replacing it, potentially thousands of times within a session, every time the reservation price or optimal spread from Chapter 3 needs to move. What looks to a retail trader like a single stable quote sitting in the depth window is, underneath, a continuous stream of cancel-and-replace messages, sent as often as the market maker's own pricing model demands.

body.text: Specific rules such as minimum disclosed quantity thresholds for iceberg orders, and freeze quantity limits per order, vary by contract and segment and are revised periodically through NSE circulars. Check the current exchange specification for the instrument in question before relying on any particular threshold in a model or system.

Every cancel-and-replace message a market maker sends has to reach the exchange, get processed, and reflect in the book, and every microsecond that takes is a microsecond during which the resting quote is technically stale relative to the market maker's own updated view. This is exactly why the next lesson, on colocation and latency, matters as much to a market making business as the pricing formulas from Chapter 3 do.

body.title: Choosing the Right Tool
body.scenario: A market maker needs to reduce a large put position built up during a volatile session, similar to Chapter 3's case study, with about 45 minutes left before expiry. It wants certainty of execution for a meaningful chunk of the position right now, without leaving any accidental resting exposure afterward, and separately wants to keep working down the rest of the position over the remaining time without revealing the full remaining size to the rest of the market.
body.prompt: Which order type fits each of the two stated goals, and why would a single plain Day limit order for the full size satisfy neither goal well?
body.modelAnswer: For the first goal, certain, immediate execution of a chunk of the position with no leftover resting exposure, an Immediate-or-Cancel order is the right tool, since it fills whatever is available right now and cancels the rest instead of leaving a stale resting order behind. For the second goal, working down the remaining size gradually while limiting how much of the true remaining quantity is visible to the market, an iceberg order using NSE's Disclosed Quantity facility fits best, showing only a small portion at a time while the rest stays hidden. A single plain Day limit order for the full remaining size would satisfy neither goal: it would rest indefinitely rather than guaranteeing an immediate fill, and it would expose the entire remaining size to the book at once, signalling exactly the kind of urgency Chapter 3 warned against.

body.title: What an IOC Order Guarantees
body.question: What does an Immediate-or-Cancel order guarantee?
options: That the entire requested quantity will always be filled
That any unfilled portion is cancelled instantly rather than resting in the book
That the order will receive a better price than a plain limit order
That the order will be hidden from other participants like an iceberg order
body.explanation: IOC guarantees no resting exposure: whatever quantity is immediately available at the specified price or better fills right away, and anything left over is cancelled instantly rather than sitting in the book. It does not guarantee the full quantity fills, does not guarantee a better price than a limit order would have gotten, and has nothing to do with hiding size, which is what an iceberg order is for.

points: Plain limit orders, continuously cancelled and replaced, are the mechanical reality behind a market maker's apparently stable two-sided quote
Immediate-or-Cancel orders fill whatever is available right now and cancel the rest instantly, making them the natural tool for a deliberate aggressive unwind with no leftover resting exposure
Iceberg orders, built on NSE's Disclosed Quantity facility, show only a portion of a large order's true size, reducing the information leakage that a single visibly large order would create

NSE's standard order validities are Day and Immediate-or-Cancel; there is no multi-day standing order, so an apparently continuous quote is really a constant stream of cancel-and-replace messages from the market maker's own system
Exact thresholds like minimum disclosed quantity and freeze limits vary by contract and are set by exchange circular, so they should be checked directly rather than assumed
Every cancel-and-replace message takes real time to reach and process at the exchange, which is exactly why the next lesson turns to colocation and latency
